title: The priest and the big bang
word: The priest and the big bang
hook: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed the expanding universe

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pope's letter that opened with a song, and a garden handed over to be kept. Your line was our common home. What one small thing did you keep? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

A man in a black clerical collar stands at a blackboard covered in equations. He is a Catholic priest. He is also a physicist, trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity. And the equations are telling him something strange. The universe isn't standing still. It's getting bigger. Run the film backward, he reasons, and everything gets closer and closer together, until it all begins from one small, dense starting point. He called it a primeval atom. Other people later gave it a nickname, and the nickname stuck. His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest. Today, the priest and the big bang.

The first line of the Bible, in the King James translation, is "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." A few lines later: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." It would be easy to hear Lemaître's idea, a universe with a beginning, and say: there it is, Genesis proved by physics. Lemaître himself didn't want anyone to say that. When church voices began to treat his theory as scientific proof of creation, he pushed back, quietly but firmly. His reasoning, as it's usually reported, ran like this. Physics describes how the universe unfolds. It can't tell you whether there is a God. And the Bible, he said, wasn't written to teach science; it was written to teach the way to salvation. Keep the two in their own lanes, and neither one has to be afraid of the other. He spent his life in both. He said Mass and he did mathematics, and he didn't think he was being torn in half. Christians have held a range of views on faith and science, and they still do. Some read Genesis as a literal account of how the world was made. Others read it as a different kind of truth, about who made the world and why. Lemaître's own path was to study the heavens as closely as he could, and to keep praying. There's an old psalm that sits well beside his blackboard: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm doesn't do the math. It looks up, and it praises.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at the sky. If it's dark, step outside or go to a window and find the night sky, even a city one with only a few stars. If it's daytime, look at the sky you have, the light and the clouds, or picture the last starry night you remember. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes go as far as they can. Far beyond what you can see, Lemaître would say, the universe is still growing. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: the heavens declare the glory of God. If you don't, simply look, and let yourself be small for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The priest and the big bang. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed that the universe is expanding from a beginning, and kept faith and science each in its own lane.
screen: `THE PRIEST AND THE BIG BANG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: faith and science. Today, when you hear the two set against each other, remember a priest at a blackboard who studied the heavens and kept praying. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians hold a range of views on how scripture and science fit together; the Catholic Church has its own academy of sciences, and Christians work as scientists across many fields.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (1927, 1931, 1951) or numbers given.
Lemaître's objection to Pius XII's 1951 address being read as scientific confirmation of creation is reported in biographies; the script says 'church voices' rather than naming the pope. Confirm.
Lemaître's view that the Bible teaches salvation, not science, is paraphrased from his reported remarks (e.g. his 1933 New York Times interview); confirm the paraphrase.
The nickname 'big bang' is attributed only to 'other people later' (usually credited to Fred Hoyle on BBC radio); confirm.
'trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity': he worked with general relativity; confirm phrasing.
Range of Christian views on Genesis and science described without ranking; confirm fairness.
howItsDone mentions the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (of which Lemaître was later president) without naming it; confirm.
